{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Saga Prefecture, Japan}}{{expand Japanese|topic=cult|田島神社|date=December 2023}} {{CS1 config|mode=cs2}} {{Infobox religious building | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = 田島神社全景.jpg | caption = View of the shrine from the sea | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|33|21|N|129|53|26|E}} | location = Japan | deity = * {{ill|Ichikishima-hime|ja|イチキシマヒメ|1=Ichikishima-hime|lt=Ichikishima-hime|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikishima-hime|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikishima-hime|qq=}} * {{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|タギツヒメ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tagitsuhime|qq=}} * {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tagorihime|qq=}} }} '''Tashima Shrine''' is a shrine situated on {{ill|Kabe Island|ja|加部島|ceb|Kabe_Shima_(pulo_sa_Hapon,_Saga-ken)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kabe Island|qq=}} in [[Yobuko, Saga|Yobuko]] Town now, [[Karatsu, Saga|Karatsu]] City, [[Saga Prefecture]], [[Japan]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QNw5D3Br8BoC&q=Tashima+Shrine |title=The Japan Magazine: A Representative Monthly of Things Japanese |date=1928 |publisher=Japan magazine Company |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hall |first=Jessica |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bmiYUKjEBMoC&q=Tashima+Shrine |title=The Deepest Edge |date=2003 |publisher=Signet |isbn=978-0-451-20796-8 |language=en}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=December 2023}} It is located in the area known as [[Matsurokoku]], which is believed to be the first land of the mainland of [[Wakoku]] as per [[Wajinden]] records. It is an important point for safe sea crossings to the continent, and has received significant orders from the central government since ancient times.
In earlier times, it was called 'Tajima Niimasu Kaminoyashiro'. It is the only [[Myojin Taisha]] in [[Hizen Province]], and was previously classified as [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kokuhei Chusha]] due to renovations during the [[Meiji era]]. Currently, it is a [[beppyo shrine]] of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-14 |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-12-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230514023648/https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |archive-date=2023-05-14 }}</ref> It is associated with [[Matsura Sayohime]] who is said to be buried on the site.<ref name="joya-1963a">{{cite book |last=Jōya |first=Moku |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=daczAQAAIAAJ&q=%22Sayohime+shrine%22 |title=Mock Jōya's Things Japanese |date=1963 |publisher=Tokyo News Service Press |page=222 |authorlink=}}</ref><ref name="the-japan-office-editors-1915a">{{Cite magazine |title=September Sights: The Season of Festivals |date=1915 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h4o0AAAAIAAJ&q=+shrines+Tajima |magazine=Japan |number=59 |page=16 |others=Based on material supplied by [[Shiga Shigetaka]] |publisher=The Japan Office}}</ref><ref name="murao-1968a">{{citation |last=Murao |first=Rikitarō |title=Tsukishi no no to Chikuhi no umi no kaiko: Nihon&kaigai shūkyō kōshō kenkyū |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fOZCAQAAIAAJ&q=望夫石 |journal=Wasada shōgaku |issue=205 |page=103 |year=1968 |script-title=ja:「筑紫の野」と「筑肥の海」の懐古―日本・海外宗教交渉略史研究― |author-link=}}</ref>
==Deities== The shrine enshrines five deities. The three primary deities are the {{ill|Three Munakata Goddesses|ja|宗像三女神|1=Three Munakata Goddesses|1=Three Munakata Goddesses|qq=Three Munakata Goddesses|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Munakata Goddesses|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Munakata Goddesses|qq=}}, who are also worshipped at {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Munakata Taisha|qq=}} and various locations throughout northern Kyushu, such as [[Usa Jingū]], Kurume, Mount Ten, and Mount Sefuri. These deities are believed to be indigenous gods from prehistory<ref name="Origin and Relationship of Tashima and Munakata Deities" />. At Tashima Shrine, they are collectively known as the "Tashima Sanshin," with {{ill|Takiribime|ja|田心姫尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|qq=}} serving as the main deity. ;Primary Deities :* {{ill|Takiribime|ja|田心姫尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|qq=}} :* {{ill|Ichikishima-hime|ja|市杵島姫尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikishima-hime|qq=}} :* {{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|湍津姫尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tagitsuhime|qq=}} ;Associated Deities :* [[Ōyamatsumi]] :* {{ill|Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto|ja|稚武王尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto|qq=}} - Son of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊|1=Yamato Takeru|lt=Prince Yamato Takeru|3=ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato Takeru|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato Takeru|qq=}} and younger brother of {{ill|Emperor Chūai|ja|仲哀天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Chūai|qq=}}.
==History==
=== Establishment ===
The exact date of establishment is unknown, though one theory suggests it dates back to the late {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}}.<ref name="Origin and Relationship of Tashima and Munakata Deities">{{Cite book|和書|title=『田島神の創祀と宗像神との関係について』 江永次男 昭和62nd year }}</ref> The site of the shrine, {{ill|Kabe Island|ja|加部島|Kabe Island=Kabe Island|lt=Kabeshima|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kabe Island|qq=}}, was once called "Himejima" or "Himekamijima" ("the island where the goddess resides").
In {{ill|Tenpyō 3|ja|天平3rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenpyō 3|qq=}} (731), {{ill|Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto|ja|稚武王尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto|qq=}} was enshrined together in the shrine. In Tenpyō 10 (738), {{ill|Emperor Shōmu|ja|聖武天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Shōmu|qq=}} issued an edict to {{ill|Ōtomo no Komaro|ja|大伴古麻呂|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtomo no Komaro|qq=}}, proclaiming the shrine's name as "Tashima Daimyōjin" (田島大明神).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|和書|title=松浦古事記|publisher=|others=寛政元年と思われる}}</ref> Some ancient texts suggest Tenpyō 3 as the shrine's founding year.
'''Enshrinement of Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto and the Kami of Upper Matsura'''
The enshrinement of Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto, the younger brother of {{ill|Emperor Chūai|ja|仲哀天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Chūai|qq=}}, is associated with a tale stating that after {{ill|Three Han Campaign|ja|三韓征伐|Three_Han_Campaign=Three Han Campaign|lt=Empress Jingū's conquest of the Three Han|ltja=神功皇后の三韓征伐|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Han Campaign|qq=}}, Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto was instructed to remain at the shrine to guard and revere it. In Tenpyō 10 (738), {{ill|Ōtomo no Komaro|ja|大伴古麻呂|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtomo no Komaro|qq=}} visited as an envoy, and around the same time, {{ill|Shijiki Shrine|ja|志々伎神社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shikizuki Shrine|qq=}}, which enshrines Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto's younger brother {{ill|Jūjōwake-Ō|ja|十城別王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jūjōwake-Ō|qq=}}, was also revered as "Matsura Daimyōjin." <ref>{{Cite book|和書|title=肥前歴史叢書８ 式内社 明神社 志々伎神社|date=1986-05-08|year=1986|publisher=芸文堂}}</ref> Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto's "Tashima Daimyōjin" and Jūjōwake-Ō's "Matsura Daimyōjin" later became known as "Upper Matsura Daimyōjin" and "Lower Matsura Daimyōjin" in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyocho|ja|延喜式神明帳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} (927). Tenpyō 10 was also the year Ōtomo no Komaro was promoted to {{ill|Ministry of War (pre-modern Japan)|ja|兵部省|1=Ministry of War (pre-modern Japan)|lt=Ministry of War|qq= (pre-modern Japan)|lt=Minister of War|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ministry of War (pre-modern Japan)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ministry of War (pre-modern Japan)|qq=}} (equivalent to the third-highest position in modern defense ministries), indicating the shrine's significance as a defense base.
* {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki|qq=}} Volume 23: {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyocho|ja|延喜式神明帳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} annotations: "Hizen Matsura District: 'Tashima is Wakatake-Ō, younger brother of Emperor Chūai, and is called Upper Matsura Daimyōjin. Shikizuki is Jūjōwake-Ō, younger brother of Wakatake-Ō, and is called Lower Matsura Daimyōjin.'"
Currently, about 2 km from Tashima Shrine, at Suginohara Ranch, there is {{ill|Hyōzuka Kofun|ja|瓢塚古墳_(唐津市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōzuka Kofun|qq=}}, designated as a historical site by Saga Prefecture. Its interior is painted red, leading to speculation that it is the tomb of Wakatake-Ō.<ref>{{Cite book|和書|title=西日本民俗文化考説|year=1988|publisher=九州大学出版会}}</ref>
== Overview ==
According to the {{ill|Shinshō Gakushōsho|ja|新抄格勅符抄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinshō Gakushōsho|qq=}}, in {{ill|Daidō 1|ja|大同元年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daidō 1|qq=}} (806), 16 households in {{ill|Hizen Province|ja|肥前国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hizen Province|qq=}} were designated as {{ill|Jinkō|ja|神戸|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinkō|qq=}}, offering taxes for the maintenance and ceremonies of "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神).
("Household" here refers to the smallest unit of registration, more akin to a village or locality rather than a single house in modern terms. These taxes were allocated to shrine repairs and ceremonies, and using them for the clergy's salary was prohibited.)
In {{ill|Enchō 5|ja|延長5th year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enchō 5|qq=}} (927), the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki|qq=}} {{ill|Jinmyōchō|ja|神名帳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmyōchō|qq=}} recorded Tashima Shrine (田嶋坐神社) as the only {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|ja|名神大社|fr|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōjin Taisha|qq=}} in Hizen Province.
During the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo period|qq=}}, it served as a place of prayer for the {{ill|Karatsu Domain|ja|唐津藩|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Karatsu Domain|qq=}}.
After the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|qq=}}, in 1871 (Meiji 4), it was Ranked as a {{ill|Kokuhei Chūsha|ja|国幣中社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kokuhei Chūsha|qq=}} under the {{ill|Modern Shrine Ranking System|ja|近代社格制度|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|1=Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Modern Shrine Ranking System|13=User:Immanuelle/Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|qq=}}. After World War II, it became a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社|1=Beppyo Shrine|2=ja|3=別表神社|4=simple|5=Beppyo Shrine|6=zh|7=別表神社|8=mr|9=बेप्प्यो तीर्थ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Beppyo Shrine|13=User:Immanuelle/Beppyo Shrine|qq=}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines.
=== Shrine Ranks ===
* {{ill|Ten'an 3|ja|天安3rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ten'an 3|qq=}} (859), January 27: Elevated from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade ({{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|qq=}}) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神). * {{ill|Jōgan 2|ja|貞観2nd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōgan 2|qq=}} (860), February 8: Elevated from Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神). * Jōgan 15 (873), September 16: Elevated from Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade to Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神). * Jōgan 18 (876), June 8: Elevated from Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade to Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神). * {{ill|Gangyō 8|ja|元慶8th year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gangyō 8|qq=}} (884), December 16: Elevated from Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade to Senior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神).
These promotions occurred around the time of the final {{ill|Kentōshi|ja|遣唐使|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kentōshi|qq=}}'s return from Tang China, reflecting the shrine's importance in international relations and its role as a representative of local shrines along Kyushu's northern coast.<ref name="Iwata Shoin" />
=== Role in Kentōshi and Kenzuishi ===
Though records of {{ill|Kentōshi|ja|遣唐使|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kentōshi|qq=}} mention Matsura Port vaguely, the shrine's high Rank relative to other prominent shrines in northern Kyushu, and its connections to imperial records, suggest it served as a representative of indigenous coastal shrines in cooperation with {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Munakata Taisha|qq=}}. Located along key routes—both the northern route (Yobuko-{{ill|Iki Island|ja|壱岐|Iki Island=Iki Island|lt=Iki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iki Island|qq=}}-{{ill|Tsushima|ja|対馬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsushima|qq=}}) and southern routes—the shrine actively participated in maritime operations. This role likely contributed to its elevated Rank.<ref name="Iwata Shoin">{{Cite book|和書|title=古代諸国神社神階制の研究|date=2002-08|year=2002|publisher=岩田書院|pages=391-395}}</ref> Its recognition in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyocho|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyocho|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} as the only Myōjin Taisha in Hizen Province, 43 years after its final promotion in 884, further highlights its importance.
== Sub-Shrines ==
[[File:20210207021831(8)b.jpg|Thumbnail|343x343px|Sayohime Shrine]] * '''Sayohime Shrine''' (佐與姫神社, also called 佐用姫神社) — Enshrines {{ill|Matsura Sayohime|ja|松浦佐用姫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsura Sayohime|qq=}}, the legendary figure of the Sayohime legend. The shrine's sacred object is a stone called "Bōfu-ishi" (望夫石), said to have transformed from Sayohime herself, and the shrine building was constructed to cover this stone.<ref name="murao" />{{sfn|Makikawa|1902|p=116}}. When {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotomi Hideyoshi|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qq=}} saw the Bōfu-ishi exposed to the elements within Tashima Shrine's grounds, he considered it too pitiable and donated land worth 100 koku to build the shrine. The donation certificate from Toyotomi Hideyoshi still exists. This land grant was continued through the Edo period under the Tokugawa shogunate.
* '''Misaki Shrine''' — The enshrined deities are {{ill|Shinatobe|ja|級長津彦神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinatobe|qq=}}, {{ill|Shinatsuhime|ja|級長津姫神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinatsuhime|qq=}}, and {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko|qq=}}. During the {{ill|Imjin War|ja|文禄・慶長の役|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imjin War|qq=}}, the warship *Kotakamaru* made seven successful voyages to the mainland and safely returned. Later, a portion of the ship's body was enshrined alongside the ship deity as a protector for maritime safety.<ref>{{Cite book|和書|title=唐津名勝案内 牧川茂太郎編|date=1902-10-10|year=1902|publisher=此村書店|page=116}}</ref>
These two shrines are uniquely rooted in the local history of the region. The main precinct of Tashima Shrine does not include branch shrines brought from prominent shrines or consolidated shrines. However, small shrines are scattered throughout the island's various districts, and during Tashima Shrine's spring prayers (*Haru Kitō*), there is a custom of visiting these small local shrines in what is called "Kusha-mairi." Additionally, it is very common for homes on the island to have small {{ill|Inari shrines|ja|稲荷社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrines|qq=}} located beside their gardens.
== Mythology == [[File:Princess Sayo at Matsu-ura.PNG|thumb|''Matsura Sayo-hime''. Caption refers to the petrification{{efn|"..{{nihongo|the vital force (''[[qi|ki]]'') of her love, in its exact original shape, transformed into stone|恋慕の気凝りて、そのままに形(かたち)石となり}}".}}{{Right|{{Small|—by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]. Series: ''Kenjo reppuden'' or "Stories of Wise and Strong Women".}}}}]]According to a version of the legend of [[Matsura Sayohime]], she prayed with such fervour that she was transformed into stone.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Pfoundes |first=C |author-link= |year=1878 |title=The Loving Wife |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ahd5yMw3Or8C&pg=PA131 |journal=The Folk-Lore Record |volume=1 |page=131 |jstor=1252349}}; {{cite book |last=Pfoundes |first=C |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TiINAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA178 |title=Fu-so Mimo Bukuro: A Budget of Japanese Notes |publisher=Japan Mai |year=1875 |location=Yokohama |page=178 |author-mask=2 |author-link=}}</ref> This petrification lore of Sayohime appears to be of later development, with its earliest attestation identified as [[renga]] poet {{illm|Bontōan|ja|梵灯庵}}'s ''Sodeshita shū'' (c. [[Ōei]] era, late 14th to early 15th century).<ref>{{citation |last=Nakayama |first=Tarō |title=Shinkō to minzoku |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t0ZfpZvZD9sC&q=佐用姫化石 |page=211 |year=1943 |script-title=ja:信仰と民俗 |chapter=Bōfuseki |chapter-url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1040027/111 |publisher=Mikasa Shobo |authorlink=:ja:中山太郎 (民俗学者) |script-chapter=ja:望夫石}} ''apud'' [[:ja:吉岡郷甫|Yoshioka, Kyōsuke]] (1906), "''Matsura Sayohime no densetsu''", ''Teikoku bungaku'' '''12''' (7).</ref> This lore of Sayohime's petrification is thought to have developed from a misunderstanding: a misreading of {{illm|Jikkinshō|ja|十訓抄|lt=''Jikkinshō''}} (13th century), which ponders on the Sayohime legend and makes reference to the petrification motif taken from an old Chinese work called the [[You Ming Lu|''Youminglu'']].{{sfnp|Yabu|2006|p=19}}<ref>{{citation |last=Ishikawa |first=Masamochi |title=Nezame no susabi 2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NANJAAAAMAAJ&pg=PP652 |work=Hyakka setsurin |volume=3 |page=642 |year=1892 |script-title=ja:ねざめのすさび 2 |publisher=Yoshikawa kobunkan |authorlink=Ishikawa Masamochi |script-work=ja:百家説林 |origyear=1805}}</ref> Sayohime's petrification is also mentioned in ''Nihon meijo monogatari'' (1670).<ref>{{harvp|Kim Kyonran|1998|pp=24–25}}; p. 21 (English abstract), ''apud'' {{harvp|Satō|1966|p=37}}</ref>
Her supposed petrified remains, an example of a {{nihongo|''bōfuseki''|望夫石|extra="rock that contemplates the husband"}},{{sfnp|Kim Kyonran|1998|pp=21–22}} is housed as the ''[[shintai]]'' ("body of the kami") at the Sayohime Shrine, an [[Setsumatsusha|undershrine]] of Tashima Shrine on Kabe Island.<ref name="joya-1963a" /><ref name="the-japan-office-editors-1915a" /><ref name="murao-1968a" /> The claim regarding her petrification on this island is given in a late account of the origin of this undershrine, preserved in the 19th-century document called the {{nihongo|''Matsura komonjo''|松浦古文書}} (written during the [[Bunka]] era).<ref name="matsura-komonjo-松浦古文書-volume-1-1934a" /> It states that the lady did not stop at the Scarf-Waving Peak bidding farewell, but she continued to a spot{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|At the place she saw the island, she called out Satehiko's name, hence the spot was named {{nihongo|''Yobu na no ura''|呼名の浦|extra=lit. the 'name-calling inlet-shore'}}, which later became the town of [[Yobuko, Saga|Yobuko]].<ref name="matsura-komonjo-松浦古文書-volume-1-1934a">''Matsura komonjo'' 松浦古文書 Volume 1('jō'), "Ch. 5: ''Sayohime jinja no koto'' 佐用姫神社之事", in: {{citation|editor-last=Yoshimura |editor-first=Shigesaburo |editor-link= |title=Matsuura zōsho |script-title=ja:「松浦叢書 |volume=1 |location=Karatsu |publisher= |year=1934 |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1214367/72 |pages=81–82}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|editor-last=Matsushiro |editor-first=Matsutarō |editor-link= |title=Higashi-Matsuura-gun shi |script-title=ja:東松浦郡史 |location=|publisher=Kyūkei-sha |year=1925 |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1020689/295 |page=559}}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia|editor= |editor-link= |title=Matsura-sayohime |script-title=ja:松浦佐用姫 まつらさよひめ |encyclopedia=Nihon daihyakka jiten (Nipponica) |location= |publisher=Shogakukan |year=1994|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%9D%BE%E6%B5%A6%E4%BD%90%E7%94%A8%E5%A7%AB-136794 |page= |isbn=}}</ref>}} from whose vantage point she beheld an island nearby. She then hopped on a fishing boat to that island, called the {{nihongo|Himekami-jima|姫神島}} island (present-day Kabe Island<ref name="yoshida-1992a">{{citation |last=Yoshida |first=Shūsaku |title=Denshō no Tsukushi-otome: Matsura Sayohime denshō |date=1992 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pgAZAQAAMAAJ&q=姫神島 |journal=Fukuoka Jogakuin University bulletin |volume=2 |page=77 |script-title=ja:伝承の〈筑紫をとめ〉-松浦佐用姫伝承- |author-link=:ja:吉田修作}}; {{citation |last=Yoshida |first=Shūsaku |title=Bungei denshōron: denshō no wotoko to wotome |date=1998 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2lE0AQAAIAAJ&q=姫神島 |page=242 |script-title=ja:文芸伝承論: 伝承の「をとこ」と「をとめ」 |location= |publisher=Ōfū |isbn=9784273030384 |author-link=:ja:吉田修作}}</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Yanagita |first=Kunio |title=Nihon densetsu meii |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2qvSAAAAMAAJ&q=%22呼名の浦%22 |page=189 |year=1971 |script-title=ja:日本伝説名彙 |location= |publisher=Nihon hōsō shuppan kyōkai |authorlink=Kunio Yanagita |origyear=1950}}</ref>) where she climbed a "bit elevated spot" and there, out of sorrow, she turned intorock.<ref name="matsura-komonjo-松浦古文書-volume-1-1934a" /> Commentators identify this elevation as the {{nihongo|Tendō-dake|天童岳}} or {{nihongo|Dentō-dake|伝登岳}}.<ref name="yoshida-1992a" />
== Festivals == (Dates listed according to the solar calendar)
=== {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} === January 1 / Held on New Year’s Day (January 1 of the Gregorian calendar), this festival celebrates the beginning of the year and prays for the nation’s safety and the protection of the people.
=== {{ill|Setsubun|ja|節分祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Setsubun|qq=}} === February 3 /
=== Spring Prayer Festival === April 1–3 / In addition to regular Shinto rituals, representatives from each district on the island visit and pray at small shrines enshrined locally in what is known as "Kusha-mairi" (district shrine visitation). Shrines such as Kinomiya, Tsuka-sama, Hiratake Shrine, Tendo Shrine (Inari), Kōshin-sama, {{ill|Hyōzuka Kofun|ja|瓢塚古墳_(唐津市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōzuka Kofun|qq=}}, Yabuso-sama, and Tenjin-sama are included as part of the visits.
=== Purification and Disaster Prevention Festival === Second Sunday of April / Known as the "Yakubarai Kigan-sai," this ceremony is conducted to purify and prevent misfortunes during years regarded as "yakudoshi" (calamitous years). These ages, calculated by traditional Japanese methods (*kazoe-doshi*), are considered turning points in physical health, family environment, or societal roles. Yakudoshi ages include 25, 42, and 61 for men, and 19, 33, and 37 for women. The years before and after these ages are referred to as "mae-yaku" (pre-yakudoshi) and "ato-yaku" (post-yakudoshi).
=== {{ill|Nagoshi-sai|ja|夏越祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi-sai|qq=}} & {{ill|Ōharae|ja|大祓|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharae|qq=}} === Last Saturday of July / While summer purification rituals are typically held within shrine precincts, Tashima Shrine’s *Nagoshi-sai* is unique in that parishioners (*ujiko*) carry a mikoshi (portable shrine) in a procession to a temporary shrine (*otabisho*) near private homes. The ritual involves welcoming the deity, spending a night together in close interaction, and receiving summer purification. (Commentary from Chief Priest Yoshiki Hirano, 1989) The size of the *chinowa* (straw ring) placed at the second torii gate on the path reflects the mikoshi's passage and is one of the largest. In earlier times, this festival was held over the last Saturday and Sunday of July, and even earlier, it was on July 29–30.
'''Historical Note:''' The exact origin of the parishioners' mikoshi procession to the *otabisho* is unknown. Photographs from the early 1960s depict the mikoshi being transported by boat to nearby Yobuko and other locations.<ref>{{Cite book|和書|title=ふるさとの民俗 佐賀の芸能・祭り|year=1967|publisher=佐賀県文化館|page=136-137}}</ref> The *otabisho* location has changed over time. In older days, it was situated on a hill near Obama Port (now Obama Park), where remnants of stone structures remain.
=== Main Festival (Reisai) === September 16 / The most important day for the shrine. Unlike many shrines where the main festival corresponds to the founding day, the founding date of Tashima Shrine is unclear, and the significance of September 16 is unknown.
=== {{ill|Niiname-sai|ja|新嘗祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niiname-sai|qq=}} === November 23 /
=== {{ill|Joya-sai|ja|除夜祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Joya-sai|qq=}} & {{ill|Ōharae|ja|大祓|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharae|qq=}} === December 31 /
== Cultural Properties ==
=== Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) === * '''Tachi (long sword)''' signed by Bitchū Province resident Yoshitsugu (artifact) – A work of the Kamakura period. Designated on April 15, 1920 (Taisho 9).<ref>{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|6401|太刀〈銘備中国住人吉次／〉}}<br />[http://www.pref.saga.lg.jp/web/data_kuni_bijyutsu01.html 国指定（美術工芸品の部）01 > 太刀（銘 備中国住人吉次）]（Saga Prefecture website）</ref>
=== Saga Prefectural Designated Cultural Properties === * '''Natural Monuments''' ''' '''Kabeshima Subtropical Plant Community''' – Designated in 1974 (Showa 49), it includes the shrine forest and the entire Kabeshima area.<ref>[http://www.pref.saga.lg.jp/web/data_ken_tennen02.html 県指定（天然記念物の部）02 > 加部島暖地性植物群落]（Saga Prefecture website）</ref>
== Miscellaneous == [[File:太閤祈念石.jpg|Thumbnail|275x275px|Taikō Memorial Stone]] * '''Hanadaka Mask''' – Signed in Shōan 2 (1300, Kamakura period). * '''Taikō Hideyoshi’s Land Donation Certificate''' – A certificate documenting the donation of 100 *koku* of land for Sayohime Shrine. * '''Taikō Memorial Stone''' – A stone linked to Toyotomi Hideyoshi's prayer for victory during the Bunroku Campaign, said to have cracked when struck with a spear. * '''Mongol Invasion Ship Anchor Stones''' – Recovered from nearby waters and enshrined. Two stones are located near the temizuya (purification basin) on the path and under the wisteria trellis inside the Zuishin Gate. * '''Hizen Torii Gate''' – Traditionally attributed to Minamoto no Yorimitsu, who served as governor of Hizen Province during the Heian period. However, repeated repairs and design changes cast doubt on this attribution, as wooden torii were standard during the Heian period. * '''Grand Staircase Torii Gate''' – Built in November 1882 (Meiji 15) by whaling community members. The plaque, reading "Tajima Shrine," was inscribed by Prince Arisugawa Taruhito, with the reverse stating, "April 27, 1882, Taruhito, First Prince." * '''Obama Port Torii Gate (First Torii Gate)''' – Built in June 1924 (Taisho 13) to commemorate Emperor Showa's wedding. The plaque, reading "Tajima Shrine," was inscribed by Prince Takahito, the head priest of Ise Shrine. The reverse includes an inscription, and an additional framed version is stored in the shrine office. * '''Great Mirror''' – Donated by Shigenobu Ōkuma, featuring a map of Japan on the back with the inscription: "June 1915, Prime Minister, Second Rank, First Class Earl Shigenobu Ōkuma."

{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Saga Prefecture, Japan}}{{expand Japanese|topic=cult|田島神社|date=December 2023}} {{CS1 config|mode=cs2}} {{Infobox religious building | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = 田島神社全景.jpg | caption = View of the shrine from the sea | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|33|21|N|129|53|26|E}} | location = Japan | deity = * {{ill|Ichikishima-hime|ja|イチキシマヒメ|1=Ichikishima-hime|lt=Ichikishima-hime|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikishima-hime|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikishima-hime|qq=}} * {{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|タギツヒメ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tagitsuhime|qq=}} * {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tagorihime|qq=}} }} '''Tashima Shrine''' is a shrine situated on {{ill|Kabe Island|ja|加部島|ceb|Kabe_Shima_(pulo_sa_Hapon,_Saga-ken)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kabe Island|qq=}} in [[Yobuko, Saga|Yobuko]] Town now, [[Karatsu, Saga|Karatsu]] City, [[Saga Prefecture]], [[Japan]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QNw5D3Br8BoC&q=Tashima+Shrine |title=The Japan Magazine: A Representative Monthly of Things Japanese |date=1928 |publisher=Japan magazine Company |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hall |first=Jessica |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bmiYUKjEBMoC&q=Tashima+Shrine |title=The Deepest Edge |date=2003 |publisher=Signet |isbn=978-0-451-20796-8 |language=en}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=December 2023}} It is located in the area known as [[Matsurokoku]], which is believed to be the first land of the mainland of [[Wakoku]] as per [[Wajinden]] records. It is an important point for safe sea crossings to the continent, and has received significant orders from the central government since ancient times.
In earlier times, it was called 'Tajima Niimasu Kaminoyashiro'. It is the only [[Myojin Taisha]] in [[Hizen Province]], and was previously classified as [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kokuhei Chusha]] due to renovations during the [[Meiji era]]. Currently, it is a [[beppyo shrine]] of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-14 |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-12-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230514023648/https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |archive-date=2023-05-14 }}</ref> It is associated with [[Matsura Sayohime]] who is said to be buried on the site.<ref name="joya-1963a">{{cite book |last=Jōya |first=Moku |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=daczAQAAIAAJ&q=%22Sayohime+shrine%22 |title=Mock Jōya's Things Japanese |date=1963 |publisher=Tokyo News Service Press |page=222 |authorlink=}}</ref><ref name="the-japan-office-editors-1915a">{{Cite magazine |title=September Sights: The Season of Festivals |date=1915 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h4o0AAAAIAAJ&q=+shrines+Tajima |magazine=Japan |number=59 |page=16 |others=Based on material supplied by [[Shiga Shigetaka]] |publisher=The Japan Office}}</ref><ref name="murao-1968a">{{citation |last=Murao |first=Rikitarō |title=Tsukishi no no to Chikuhi no umi no kaiko: Nihon&kaigai shūkyō kōshō kenkyū |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fOZCAQAAIAAJ&q=望夫石 |journal=Wasada shōgaku |issue=205 |page=103 |year=1968 |script-title=ja:「筑紫の野」と「筑肥の海」の懐古―日本・海外宗教交渉略史研究― |author-link=}}</ref>
==Deities== The shrine enshrines five deities. The three primary deities are the {{ill|Three Munakata Goddesses|ja|宗像三女神|1=Three Munakata Goddesses|1=Three Munakata Goddesses|qq=Three Munakata Goddesses|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Munakata Goddesses|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Munakata Goddesses|qq=}}, who are also worshipped at {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Munakata Taisha|qq=}} and various locations throughout northern Kyushu, such as [[Usa Jingū]], Kurume, Mount Ten, and Mount Sefuri. These deities are believed to be indigenous gods from prehistory<ref name="Origin and Relationship of Tashima and Munakata Deities" />. At Tashima Shrine, they are collectively known as the "Tashima Sanshin," with {{ill|Takiribime|ja|田心姫尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|qq=}} serving as the main deity. ;Primary Deities :* {{ill|Takiribime|ja|田心姫尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|qq=}} :* {{ill|Ichikishima-hime|ja|市杵島姫尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikishima-hime|qq=}} :* {{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|湍津姫尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tagitsuhime|qq=}} ;Associated Deities :* [[Ōyamatsumi]] :* {{ill|Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto|ja|稚武王尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto|qq=}} - Son of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊|1=Yamato Takeru|lt=Prince Yamato Takeru|3=ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato Takeru|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato Takeru|qq=}} and younger brother of {{ill|Emperor Chūai|ja|仲哀天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Chūai|qq=}}.
==History==
=== Establishment ===
The exact date of establishment is unknown, though one theory suggests it dates back to the late {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}}.<ref name="Origin and Relationship of Tashima and Munakata Deities">{{Cite book|和書|title=『田島神の創祀と宗像神との関係について』 江永次男 昭和62nd year }}</ref> The site of the shrine, {{ill|Kabe Island|ja|加部島|Kabe Island=Kabe Island|lt=Kabeshima|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kabe Island|qq=}}, was once called "Himejima" or "Himekamijima" ("the island where the goddess resides").
In {{ill|Tenpyō 3|ja|天平3rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenpyō 3|qq=}} (731), {{ill|Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto|ja|稚武王尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto|qq=}} was enshrined together in the shrine. In Tenpyō 10 (738), {{ill|Emperor Shōmu|ja|聖武天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Shōmu|qq=}} issued an edict to {{ill|Ōtomo no Komaro|ja|大伴古麻呂|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtomo no Komaro|qq=}}, proclaiming the shrine's name as "Tashima Daimyōjin" (田島大明神).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|和書|title=松浦古事記|publisher=|others=寛政元年と思われる}}</ref> Some ancient texts suggest Tenpyō 3 as the shrine's founding year.
'''Enshrinement of Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto and the Kami of Upper Matsura'''
The enshrinement of Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto, the younger brother of {{ill|Emperor Chūai|ja|仲哀天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Chūai|qq=}}, is associated with a tale stating that after {{ill|Three Han Campaign|ja|三韓征伐|Three_Han_Campaign=Three Han Campaign|lt=Empress Jingū's conquest of the Three Han|ltja=神功皇后の三韓征伐|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Han Campaign|qq=}}, Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto was instructed to remain at the shrine to guard and revere it. In Tenpyō 10 (738), {{ill|Ōtomo no Komaro|ja|大伴古麻呂|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtomo no Komaro|qq=}} visited as an envoy, and around the same time, {{ill|Shijiki Shrine|ja|志々伎神社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shikizuki Shrine|qq=}}, which enshrines Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto's younger brother {{ill|Jūjōwake-Ō|ja|十城別王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jūjōwake-Ō|qq=}}, was also revered as "Matsura Daimyōjin." <ref>{{Cite book|和書|title=肥前歴史叢書８ 式内社 明神社 志々伎神社|date=1986-05-08|year=1986|publisher=芸文堂}}</ref> Wakatake-Ō-Mikoto's "Tashima Daimyōjin" and Jūjōwake-Ō's "Matsura Daimyōjin" later became known as "Upper Matsura Daimyōjin" and "Lower Matsura Daimyōjin" in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神明帳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} (927). Tenpyō 10 was also the year Ōtomo no Komaro was promoted to {{ill|Ministry of War (pre-modern Japan)|ja|兵部省|1=Ministry of War (pre-modern Japan)|lt=Ministry of War|qq= (pre-modern Japan)|lt=Minister of War|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ministry of War (pre-modern Japan)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ministry of War (pre-modern Japan)|qq=}} (equivalent to the third-highest position in modern defense ministries), indicating the shrine's significance as a defense base.
* {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki|qq=}} Volume 23: {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神明帳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} annotations: "Hizen Matsura District: 'Tashima is Wakatake-Ō, younger brother of Emperor Chūai, and is called Upper Matsura Daimyōjin. Shikizuki is Jūjōwake-Ō, younger brother of Wakatake-Ō, and is called Lower Matsura Daimyōjin.'"
Currently, about 2 km from Tashima Shrine, at Suginohara Ranch, there is {{ill|Hyōzuka Kofun|ja|瓢塚古墳_(唐津市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōzuka Kofun|qq=}}, designated as a historical site by Saga Prefecture. Its interior is painted red, leading to speculation that it is the tomb of Wakatake-Ō.<ref>{{Cite book|和書|title=西日本民俗文化考説|year=1988|publisher=九州大学出版会}}</ref>
== Overview ==
According to the {{ill|Shinshō Gakushōsho|ja|新抄格勅符抄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinshō Gakushōsho|qq=}}, in {{ill|Daidō 1|ja|大同元年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daidō 1|qq=}} (806), 16 households in {{ill|Hizen Province|ja|肥前国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hizen Province|qq=}} were designated as {{ill|Jinkō|ja|神戸|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinkō|qq=}}, offering taxes for the maintenance and ceremonies of "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神).
("Household" here refers to the smallest unit of registration, more akin to a village or locality rather than a single house in modern terms. These taxes were allocated to shrine repairs and ceremonies, and using them for the clergy's salary was prohibited.)
In {{ill|Enchō 5|ja|延長5th year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enchō 5|qq=}} (927), the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki|qq=}} {{ill|Jinmyōchō|ja|神名帳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmyōchō|qq=}} recorded Tashima Shrine (田嶋坐神社) as the only {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|ja|名神大社|fr|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōjin Taisha|qq=}} in Hizen Province.
During the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo period|qq=}}, it served as a place of prayer for the {{ill|Karatsu Domain|ja|唐津藩|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Karatsu Domain|qq=}}.
After the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|qq=}}, in 1871 (Meiji 4), it was Ranked as a {{ill|Kokuhei Chūsha|ja|国幣中社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kokuhei Chūsha|qq=}} under the {{ill|Modern Shrine Ranking System|ja|近代社格制度|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|1=Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Modern Shrine Ranking System|13=User:Immanuelle/Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|qq=}}. After World War II, it became a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社|1=Beppyo Shrine|2=ja|3=別表神社|4=simple|5=Beppyo Shrine|6=zh|7=別表神社|8=mr|9=बेप्प्यो तीर्थ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Beppyo Shrine|13=User:Immanuelle/Beppyo Shrine|qq=}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines.
=== Shrine Ranks ===
* {{ill|Ten'an 3|ja|天安3rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ten'an 3|qq=}} (859), January 27: Elevated from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade ({{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|qq=}}) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神). * {{ill|Jōgan 2|ja|貞観2nd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōgan 2|qq=}} (860), February 8: Elevated from Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神). * Jōgan 15 (873), September 16: Elevated from Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade to Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神). * Jōgan 18 (876), June 8: Elevated from Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade to Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神). * {{ill|Gangyō 8|ja|元慶8th year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gangyō 8|qq=}} (884), December 16: Elevated from Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade to Senior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) - Written as "Tashima Kami" (田嶋神).
These promotions occurred around the time of the final {{ill|Kentōshi|ja|遣唐使|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kentōshi|qq=}}'s return from Tang China, reflecting the shrine's importance in international relations and its role as a representative of local shrines along Kyushu's northern coast.<ref name="Iwata Shoin" />
=== Role in Kentōshi and Kenzuishi ===
Though records of {{ill|Kentōshi|ja|遣唐使|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kentōshi|qq=}} mention Matsura Port vaguely, the shrine's high Rank relative to other prominent shrines in northern Kyushu, and its connections to imperial records, suggest it served as a representative of indigenous coastal shrines in cooperation with {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Munakata Taisha|qq=}}. Located along key routes—both the northern route (Yobuko-{{ill|Iki Island|ja|壱岐|Iki Island=Iki Island|lt=Iki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iki Island|qq=}}-{{ill|Tsushima|ja|対馬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsushima|qq=}}) and southern routes—the shrine actively participated in maritime operations. This role likely contributed to its elevated Rank.<ref name="Iwata Shoin">{{Cite book|和書|title=古代諸国神社神階制の研究|date=2002-08|year=2002|publisher=岩田書院|pages=391-395}}</ref> Its recognition in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} as the only Myōjin Taisha in Hizen Province, 43 years after its final promotion in 884, further highlights its importance.
== Sub-Shrines ==
[[File:20210207021831(8)b.jpg|Thumbnail|343x343px|Sayohime Shrine]] * '''Sayohime Shrine''' (佐與姫神社, also called 佐用姫神社) — Enshrines {{ill|Matsura Sayohime|ja|松浦佐用姫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsura Sayohime|qq=}}, the legendary figure of the Sayohime legend. The shrine's sacred object is a stone called "Bōfu-ishi" (望夫石), said to have transformed from Sayohime herself, and the shrine building was constructed to cover this stone.<ref name="murao" />{{sfn|Makikawa|1902|p=116}}. When {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotomi Hideyoshi|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qq=}} saw the Bōfu-ishi exposed to the elements within Tashima Shrine's grounds, he considered it too pitiable and donated land worth 100 koku to build the shrine. The donation certificate from Toyotomi Hideyoshi still exists. This land grant was continued through the Edo period under the Tokugawa shogunate.
* '''Misaki Shrine''' — The enshrined deities are {{ill|Shinatobe|ja|級長津彦神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinatobe|qq=}}, {{ill|Shinatsuhime|ja|級長津姫神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinatsuhime|qq=}}, and {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko|qq=}}. During the {{ill|Imjin War|ja|文禄・慶長の役|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imjin War|qq=}}, the warship *Kotakamaru* made seven successful voyages to the mainland and safely returned. Later, a portion of the ship's body was enshrined alongside the ship deity as a protector for maritime safety.<ref>{{Cite book|和書|title=唐津名勝案内 牧川茂太郎編|date=1902-10-10|year=1902|publisher=此村書店|page=116}}</ref>
These two shrines are uniquely rooted in the local history of the region. The main precinct of Tashima Shrine does not include branch shrines brought from prominent shrines or consolidated shrines. However, small shrines are scattered throughout the island's various districts, and during Tashima Shrine's spring prayers (*Haru Kitō*), there is a custom of visiting these small local shrines in what is called "Kusha-mairi." Additionally, it is very common for homes on the island to have small {{ill|Inari shrines|ja|稲荷社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrines|qq=}} located beside their gardens.
== Mythology == [[File:Princess Sayo at Matsu-ura.PNG|thumb|''Matsura Sayo-hime''. Caption refers to the petrification{{efn|"..{{nihongo|the vital force (''[[qi|ki]]'') of her love, in its exact original shape, transformed into stone|恋慕の気凝りて、そのままに形(かたち)石となり}}".}}{{Right|{{Small|—by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]. Series: ''Kenjo reppuden'' or "Stories of Wise and Strong Women".}}}}]]According to a version of the legend of [[Matsura Sayohime]], she prayed with such fervour that she was transformed into stone.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Pfoundes |first=C |author-link= |year=1878 |title=The Loving Wife |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ahd5yMw3Or8C&pg=PA131 |journal=The Folk-Lore Record |volume=1 |page=131 |jstor=1252349}}; {{cite book |last=Pfoundes |first=C |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TiINAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA178 |title=Fu-so Mimo Bukuro: A Budget of Japanese Notes |publisher=Japan Mai |year=1875 |location=Yokohama |page=178 |author-mask=2 |author-link=}}</ref> This petrification lore of Sayohime appears to be of later development, with its earliest attestation identified as [[renga]] poet {{illm|Bontōan|ja|梵灯庵}}'s ''Sodeshita shū'' (c. [[Ōei]] era, late 14th to early 15th century).<ref>{{citation |last=Nakayama |first=Tarō |title=Shinkō to minzoku |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t0ZfpZvZD9sC&q=佐用姫化石 |page=211 |year=1943 |script-title=ja:信仰と民俗 |chapter=Bōfuseki |chapter-url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1040027/111 |publisher=Mikasa Shobo |authorlink=:ja:中山太郎 (民俗学者) |script-chapter=ja:望夫石}} ''apud'' [[:ja:吉岡郷甫|Yoshioka, Kyōsuke]] (1906), "''Matsura Sayohime no densetsu''", ''Teikoku bungaku'' '''12''' (7).</ref> This lore of Sayohime's petrification is thought to have developed from a misunderstanding: a misreading of {{illm|Jikkinshō|ja|十訓抄|lt=''Jikkinshō''}} (13th century), which ponders on the Sayohime legend and makes reference to the petrification motif taken from an old Chinese work called the [[You Ming Lu|''Youminglu'']].{{sfnp|Yabu|2006|p=19}}<ref>{{citation |last=Ishikawa |first=Masamochi |title=Nezame no susabi 2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NANJAAAAMAAJ&pg=PP652 |work=Hyakka setsurin |volume=3 |page=642 |year=1892 |script-title=ja:ねざめのすさび 2 |publisher=Yoshikawa kobunkan |authorlink=Ishikawa Masamochi |script-work=ja:百家説林 |origyear=1805}}</ref> Sayohime's petrification is also mentioned in ''Nihon meijo monogatari'' (1670).<ref>{{harvp|Kim Kyonran|1998|pp=24–25}}; p. 21 (English abstract), ''apud'' {{harvp|Satō|1966|p=37}}</ref>
Her supposed petrified remains, an example of a {{nihongo|''bōfuseki''|望夫石|extra="rock that contemplates the husband"}},{{sfnp|Kim Kyonran|1998|pp=21–22}} is housed as the ''[[shintai]]'' ("body of the kami") at the Sayohime Shrine, an [[Setsumatsusha|undershrine]] of Tashima Shrine on Kabe Island.<ref name="joya-1963a" /><ref name="the-japan-office-editors-1915a" /><ref name="murao-1968a" /> The claim regarding her petrification on this island is given in a late account of the origin of this undershrine, preserved in the 19th-century document called the {{nihongo|''Matsura komonjo''|松浦古文書}} (written during the [[Bunka]] era).<ref name="matsura-komonjo-松浦古文書-volume-1-1934a" /> It states that the lady did not stop at the Scarf-Waving Peak bidding farewell, but she continued to a spot{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|At the place she saw the island, she called out Satehiko's name, hence the spot was named {{nihongo|''Yobu na no ura''|呼名の浦|extra=lit. the 'name-calling inlet-shore'}}, which later became the town of [[Yobuko, Saga|Yobuko]].<ref name="matsura-komonjo-松浦古文書-volume-1-1934a">''Matsura komonjo'' 松浦古文書 Volume 1('jō'), "Ch. 5: ''Sayohime jinja no koto'' 佐用姫神社之事", in: {{citation|editor-last=Yoshimura |editor-first=Shigesaburo |editor-link= |title=Matsuura zōsho |script-title=ja:「松浦叢書 |volume=1 |location=Karatsu |publisher= |year=1934 |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1214367/72 |pages=81–82}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|editor-last=Matsushiro |editor-first=Matsutarō |editor-link= |title=Higashi-Matsuura-gun shi |script-title=ja:東松浦郡史 |location=|publisher=Kyūkei-sha |year=1925 |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1020689/295 |page=559}}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia|editor= |editor-link= |title=Matsura-sayohime |script-title=ja:松浦佐用姫 まつらさよひめ |encyclopedia=Nihon daihyakka jiten (Nipponica) |location= |publisher=Shogakukan |year=1994|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%9D%BE%E6%B5%A6%E4%BD%90%E7%94%A8%E5%A7%AB-136794 |page= |isbn=}}</ref>}} from whose vantage point she beheld an island nearby. She then hopped on a fishing boat to that island, called the {{nihongo|Himekami-jima|姫神島}} island (present-day Kabe Island<ref name="yoshida-1992a">{{citation |last=Yoshida |first=Shūsaku |title=Denshō no Tsukushi-otome: Matsura Sayohime denshō |date=1992 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pgAZAQAAMAAJ&q=姫神島 |journal=Fukuoka Jogakuin University bulletin |volume=2 |page=77 |script-title=ja:伝承の〈筑紫をとめ〉-松浦佐用姫伝承- |author-link=:ja:吉田修作}}; {{citation |last=Yoshida |first=Shūsaku |title=Bungei denshōron: denshō no wotoko to wotome |date=1998 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2lE0AQAAIAAJ&q=姫神島 |page=242 |script-title=ja:文芸伝承論: 伝承の「をとこ」と「をとめ」 |location= |publisher=Ōfū |isbn=9784273030384 |author-link=:ja:吉田修作}}</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Yanagita |first=Kunio |title=Nihon densetsu meii |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2qvSAAAAMAAJ&q=%22呼名の浦%22 |page=189 |year=1971 |script-title=ja:日本伝説名彙 |location= |publisher=Nihon hōsō shuppan kyōkai |authorlink=Kunio Yanagita |origyear=1950}}</ref>) where she climbed a "bit elevated spot" and there, out of sorrow, she turned intorock.<ref name="matsura-komonjo-松浦古文書-volume-1-1934a" /> Commentators identify this elevation as the {{nihongo|Tendō-dake|天童岳}} or {{nihongo|Dentō-dake|伝登岳}}.<ref name="yoshida-1992a" />
== Festivals == (Dates listed according to the solar calendar)
=== {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} === January 1 / Held on New Year’s Day (January 1 of the Gregorian calendar), this festival celebrates the beginning of the year and prays for the nation’s safety and the protection of the people.
=== {{ill|Setsubun|ja|節分祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Setsubun|qq=}} === February 3 /
=== Spring Prayer Festival === April 1–3 / In addition to regular Shinto rituals, representatives from each district on the island visit and pray at small shrines enshrined locally in what is known as "Kusha-mairi" (district shrine visitation). Shrines such as Kinomiya, Tsuka-sama, Hiratake Shrine, Tendo Shrine (Inari), Kōshin-sama, {{ill|Hyōzuka Kofun|ja|瓢塚古墳_(唐津市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōzuka Kofun|qq=}}, Yabuso-sama, and Tenjin-sama are included as part of the visits.
=== Purification and Disaster Prevention Festival === Second Sunday of April / Known as the "Yakubarai Kigan-sai," this ceremony is conducted to purify and prevent misfortunes during years regarded as "yakudoshi" (calamitous years). These ages, calculated by traditional Japanese methods (*kazoe-doshi*), are considered turning points in physical health, family environment, or societal roles. Yakudoshi ages include 25, 42, and 61 for men, and 19, 33, and 37 for women. The years before and after these ages are referred to as "mae-yaku" (pre-yakudoshi) and "ato-yaku" (post-yakudoshi).
=== {{ill|Nagoshi-sai|ja|夏越祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi-sai|qq=}} & {{ill|Ōharae|ja|大祓|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharae|qq=}} === Last Saturday of July / While summer purification rituals are typically held within shrine precincts, Tashima Shrine’s *Nagoshi-sai* is unique in that parishioners (*ujiko*) carry a mikoshi (portable shrine) in a procession to a temporary shrine (*otabisho*) near private homes. The ritual involves welcoming the deity, spending a night together in close interaction, and receiving summer purification. (Commentary from Chief Priest Yoshiki Hirano, 1989) The size of the *chinowa* (straw ring) placed at the second torii gate on the path reflects the mikoshi's passage and is one of the largest. In earlier times, this festival was held over the last Saturday and Sunday of July, and even earlier, it was on July 29–30.
'''Historical Note:''' The exact origin of the parishioners' mikoshi procession to the *otabisho* is unknown. Photographs from the early 1960s depict the mikoshi being transported by boat to nearby Yobuko and other locations.<ref>{{Cite book|和書|title=ふるさとの民俗 佐賀の芸能・祭り|year=1967|publisher=佐賀県文化館|page=136-137}}</ref> The *otabisho* location has changed over time. In older days, it was situated on a hill near Obama Port (now Obama Park), where remnants of stone structures remain.
=== Main Festival (Reisai) === September 16 / The most important day for the shrine. Unlike many shrines where the main festival corresponds to the founding day, the founding date of Tashima Shrine is unclear, and the significance of September 16 is unknown.
=== {{ill|Niiname-sai|ja|新嘗祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niiname-sai|qq=}} === November 23 /
=== {{ill|Joya-sai|ja|除夜祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Joya-sai|qq=}} & {{ill|Ōharae|ja|大祓|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharae|qq=}} === December 31 /
== Cultural Properties ==
=== Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) === * '''Tachi (long sword)''' signed by Bitchū Province resident Yoshitsugu (artifact) – A work of the Kamakura period. Designated on April 15, 1920 (Taisho 9).<ref>{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|6401|太刀〈銘備中国住人吉次／〉}}<br />[http://www.pref.saga.lg.jp/web/data_kuni_bijyutsu01.html 国指定（美術工芸品の部）01 > 太刀（銘 備中国住人吉次）]（Saga Prefecture website）</ref>
=== Saga Prefectural Designated Cultural Properties === * '''Natural Monuments''' ''' '''Kabeshima Subtropical Plant Community''' – Designated in 1974 (Showa 49), it includes the shrine forest and the entire Kabeshima area.<ref>[http://www.pref.saga.lg.jp/web/data_ken_tennen02.html 県指定（天然記念物の部）02 > 加部島暖地性植物群落]（Saga Prefecture website）</ref>
== Miscellaneous == [[File:太閤祈念石.jpg|Thumbnail|275x275px|Taikō Memorial Stone]] * '''Hanadaka Mask''' – Signed in Shōan 2 (1300, Kamakura period). * '''Taikō Hideyoshi’s Land Donation Certificate''' – A certificate documenting the donation of 100 *koku* of land for Sayohime Shrine. * '''Taikō Memorial Stone''' – A stone linked to Toyotomi Hideyoshi's prayer for victory during the Bunroku Campaign, said to have cracked when struck with a spear. * '''Mongol Invasion Ship Anchor Stones''' – Recovered from nearby waters and enshrined. Two stones are located near the temizuya (purification basin) on the path and under the wisteria trellis inside the Zuishin Gate. * '''Hizen Torii Gate''' – Traditionally attributed to Minamoto no Yorimitsu, who served as governor of Hizen Province during the Heian period. However, repeated repairs and design changes cast doubt on this attribution, as wooden torii were standard during the Heian period. * '''Grand Staircase Torii Gate''' – Built in November 1882 (Meiji 15) by whaling community members. The plaque, reading "Tajima Shrine," was inscribed by Prince Arisugawa Taruhito, with the reverse stating, "April 27, 1882, Taruhito, First Prince." * '''Obama Port Torii Gate (First Torii Gate)''' – Built in June 1924 (Taisho 13) to commemorate Emperor Showa's wedding. The plaque, reading "Tajima Shrine," was inscribed by Prince Takahito, the head priest of Ise Shrine. The reverse includes an inscription, and an additional framed version is stored in the shrine office. * '''Great Mirror''' – Donated by Shigenobu Ōkuma, featuring a map of Japan on the back with the inscription: "June 1915, Prime Minister, Second Rank, First Class Earl Shigenobu Ōkuma."
